summary_html: Any person (not just mandated reporters) may submit a **voluntary report** to child-protection authorities. CAPTA requires states to maintain mechanisms for intake, confidentiality, and immunity policies tied to federal funding.
authority_html: - **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — requires states to operate intake/report systems that accept voluntary reports and protect good-faith reporters

primary_citations.citation_text: Hawaii — HRS Chapter 587A, Child Protective Act
Haw. Rev. Stat. § 350-1.1, Reports (persons required to report child abuse or neglect)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Kaho'ohanohano ex rel. Morales-Kaho'ohanohano v. Department of Human Services
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed a negligence judgment against DHS, holding that once DHS receives a report of suspected child abuse, HRS chapter 587 and its implementing rules create a special relationship and an affirmative legal duty to investigate reasonably and to protect the reported child from further harm.
key_cases.relevance: A report from any source, once received, creates the same special relationship and protective duty, so third-party reports carry the same downstream legal consequence.
key_cases.quote: Accordingly, we conclude that DHS had a duty to protect Minor under the circumstances of this case.

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause imposes no general affirmative federal duty on a State to protect a child from private violence, even where caseworkers received and recorded repeated reports of abuse, while noting that States may impose such duties through their own tort law.
key_cases.relevance: Federal § 1983 liability will not follow from an ignored third-party report absent custody or a state-created danger.
key_cases.quote: As a general matter, then, we conclude that a State's failure to protect an individual against private violence simply does not constitute a violation of the Due Process Clause.

key_cases.court: Intermediate Court of Appeals of Hawai'i
key_cases.holding: The ICA affirmed an order of family supervision, holding that a chapter 587 petition is verified by a declaration under penalty of perjury, that threatened harm alone suffices to sustain the petition, and that DHS's disclosure of case information to the police was not a ground for dismissal absent particularized objection.
key_cases.relevance: Reports of threatened harm from any source can support court intervention without proof of an accomplished injury.
key_cases.quote: Thus, allegations of actual harm are not required to sustain a petition for family supervision and allegations of threatened harm would suffice.

state_agency.name: Hawaii Department of Human Services, Child Welfare Services
state_agency.hotline: 808-832-5300 (Oahu) or toll-free 1-888-380-3088 (Hawaii Island, Maui, Molokai, Lanai, Kauai), 24 hours a day, 7 days a week

mandatory_reporters: Licensed or registered professionals of the healing arts or any health-related occupation who examine, attend, treat, or provide other professional or specialized services, including but not limited to physicians (including physicians in training), psychologists, dentists, nurses, osteopathic physicians and surgeons, optometrists, chiropractors, podiatrists, pharmacists, and other health-related professionals
Employees or officers of any public or private school
Employees or officers of any public or private agency or institution, or other individuals, providing social, medical, hospital, or mental health services, including financial assistance

Employees or officers of any law enforcement agency, including but not limited to the courts, police departments, department of law enforcement, correctional institutions, and parole or probation offices
Individual providers of child care, or employees or officers of any licensed or registered child care facility, foster home, or similar institution
Employees of any public or private agency providing recreational or sports activities
Commercial film and photographic print or image processors

Members of the clergy or custodians of records therefor; a member of the clergy is not required to report information gained solely during a penitential communication, except when the clergy member believes that there exists a substantial risk that child abuse or neglect that is especially heinous, atrocious, or cruel, manifesting exceptional depravity, may occur in the reasonably foreseeable future, and a clergy member who receives reportable information from any source other than a penitential communication must report it regardless of whether the same information was also received during a penitential communication
reporting_details: Hawaii is not a universal-reporting state: only the ten categories of persons listed in Haw. Rev. Stat. § 350-1.1(a) must report, and they must report the matter immediately and orally to the Department of Human Services or the police, with a written report to follow (§ 350-1.1(c)); anyone else may report voluntarily under § 350-1.3.
